title: Why America Sorts Itself
hook: Red places get redder and blue places get bluer. Is it because people move to match their politics — or is politics just one reason among many?
key_points: 'Ideological sorting' is the idea that people increasingly live among neighbors who share their politics, deepening the red-blue divide.
The divide between red and blue places is real and shows up across many parts of life, not just elections.
Recent research suggests people rarely move for politics alone — jobs, taxes, safety, cost of living and family usually weigh more.
Politics often rides along with those practical factors rather than driving the move by itself.
So geographic polarization may be partly a byproduct of ordinary life choices, not just deliberate political clustering.
content_html: It's become a familiar story about American politics: people are clustering into like-minded communities, so red areas grow redder and blue areas bluer. The pattern even has a name — "ideological sorting." But why it happens turns out to be more tangled than the tidy version suggests.
extra_html: As NPR's Scott Neuman reports, the red-state/blue-state divide is real and shows up across many parts of life, not just elections. The open question is what drives it. Recent research suggests that few people actually pick up and move purely to be around others who share their politics. Far more often, the decision turns on practical concerns — job opportunities, taxes, public safety, the cost of living, or being near family — and political preference is just one factor riding along with the rest. That reframes the divide: geographic polarization may be less a deliberate sorting by ideology than a side effect of ordinary choices that happen to correlate with politics. Understanding that distinction matters for anyone trying to explain — or bridge — the gap. (U.S. example, though similar dynamics appear in other democracies.)

related.title: Political Parties & Party Systems
related.hook: Parties are how scattered voters become an organized choice. Whether a country has two big ones or a dozen shapes how its whole politics feels.

related.title: Districts & Gerrymandering
related.hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.

related.title: The Left–Right Spectrum
related.hook: "Left" and "right" are political shorthand the whole world uses — but they began as nothing more than which side of a room people sat on.

A deliberate desire to live only among people who share one's politics
Random chance unrelated to any preference

flashcards.explanation_html: The research finds people rarely move for politics alone; political preference usually rides along with practical reasons.

It proves the red-blue divide isn't real

flashcards.explanation_html: The divide is real, but the research suggests many factors drive it, changing how we explain — and try to bridge — the gap.
